claims.claim: Hong Kong should extend and enforce the cap on rent increases within a tenancy, paired with tenure security and funded inspections.
Hong Kong should not introduce a hard cap on initial rents.
The type of rent control matters more than how strict it is.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units, mostly new arrivals, single-parent families, and people waiting for public housing.
Subdivided unit tenants pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot compared with ordinary flats.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance caps increases within a tenancy but not the starting rent.
The estimated stock of subdivided units grew from 100,800 in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025, including after the 2021 ordinance.
First-generation rent controls that cap rent levels consistently reduce stock, while second-generation controls that cap increases show small or null effects.
A 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents gives incumbents about 900 dollars a month while 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot enter the segment.
After Berlin's 2020 rent cap, listings fell and when the law was struck down rents jumped above the earlier trend.
An NGO survey of 440 households found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three years of tenure security.
The NGO report argues that a rent cap treats the price symptom of a quantity problem and diverts enforcement spending from fire and ventilation inspections.
The NGO report itself supports a narrow tightening with tenure security and a light band on initial rents.
The landlords' association admits it has no data on members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate.
Inspection covers under 6 percent of subdivided unit stock, and a certifiable tenancy register would need 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would miss the most exploited tenants, those without written agreements and the newest arrivals.
Rent burden rose from 31 to 34 percent of income even under the ordinance.
Tightening should mean bringing more units under the increase cap, funding the register and inspections, and giving tenants real security.
A hard cap on initial rents is not worth the supply risk.

cites.sentence: About 110,000 households live in subdivided units, and they are mostly new arrivals, single-parent families and people waiting for public housing, where the wait is around five and a half years [D1p2].
They also pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot compared with ordinary flats [D1p1].
Hong Kong already has one tool, the 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance, which caps increases within a tenancy but not the starting rent [D1p3].
The estimated stock of subdivided units grew from 100,800 in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025, including after the 2021 ordinance [D2p1].
The working paper explains why: first-generation controls, which cap rent levels, consistently reduce stock, while second-generation controls, which cap increases, show small or null effects [D6p2].

The paper estimates that a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1], and it models a 15 percent cut in initial rents as giving incumbents about 900 dollars a month while 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot enter the segment [D6p4].

The paper estimates that a 10 percent cap-induced rent cut removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1], and it models a 15 percent cut in initial rents as giving incumbents about 900 dollars a month while 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot enter the segment [D6p4].
After its 2020 cap, listings fell as owners withheld or moved flats to other segments, and when the law was struck down rents jumped above the earlier trend [D7p1][D7p2].
After its 2020 cap, listings fell as owners withheld or moved flats to other segments, and when the law was struck down rents jumped above the earlier trend [D7p1][D7p2].
The lesson is that caps protect those already inside and the bill goes to those outside [D7p3].
It surveyed 440 households and found 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three years of tenure security [D11p1].
It argues that a cap treats the price symptom of a quantity problem, because the queue is long, and that enforcement spent on rents is not spent on fire and ventilation inspections [D11p2].
The report itself supports a narrow tightening with tenure security and a light band on initial rents [D11p3], so even the NGO accepts some price limit.
They call a hard cap confiscatory and promise to exit if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p1][D5p2].
They call a hard cap confiscatory and promise to exit if returns fall below mortgage cost [D5p1][D5p2].
The association admits it has no data on members' actual margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate [D5p3].
Inspection covers under 6 percent of stock, and a certifiable tenancy register would need 40 to 60 staff-years [D10p1].
Worse, the tenants least able to complain are those without written agreements and the newest arrivals, so enforcement would miss the most exploited group [D10p2].
The committee could not find a design that protects them first rather than last [D10p3].
Data is also thin: reporting of new tenancy terms is voluntary below the ordinance threshold, so recent figures are extrapolated [D2p3].
And rent burden still rose from 31 to 34 percent of income even under the ordinance [D2p2].
